With the field voltage held constant, the generator is disconnected from the transmission line. In steady state, how does the magnitude of the generator terminal voltage change?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows a synchronous generator connected through a switch/circuit breaker to a long transmission line labeled "Long Transmission Line", with the right side being the receiving end, appearing as an open circuit at the line end. Reasoning: a long lossless transmission line, when open-circuited at the receiving end, will still absorb line charging current, equivalent to the generator terminal being connected to a capacitive load, so the current leads the terminal voltage. When keeping the excitation voltage unchanged, the internal potential E of the synchronous generator can approximately be regarded as unchanged. The generator phasor equation can be written as E = V + jX_s I. Since the capacitive leading current makes jX_s I opposite to the direction of the terminal voltage, when the line is connected the terminal voltage V will be higher than the terminal voltage corresponding to the no-load internal potential. After disconnecting the line, the stator current I becomes zero, and the terminal voltage returns to the no-load value V = E. Therefore, relative to when connected to the long open-circuited line, the magnitude of the generator terminal voltage will decrease.

method.method_draft: Identify the open long lossless line as a capacitive load drawing leading charging current. With constant field voltage, treat the generator internal emf as fixed. Apply the synchronous-generator phasor equation while connected to the line, then set the stator current to zero after disconnection. Since the leading capacitive current made the terminal voltage higher than the no-load internal emf, removing the line makes the terminal voltage drop to the no-load value.

planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Model a long lossless open-circuited line at steady state as presenting mainly shunt capacitance/charging current to the generator. For a generator, use the phasor relation E = V + jX_s I with field excitation fixed, so E is fixed. The capacitive line current leads V; taking I ≈ jB V gives jX_s I = -X_s B V, so E = V(1 - X_s B), implying the connected terminal voltage is greater than the no-load value E. After disconnection, I = 0 and V = E. Therefore the terminal voltage magnitude decreases.

When the line is removed, the charging current and its voltage-boosting effect disappear while excitation remains unchanged, so the steady terminal voltage is lower.
